title: Amendment 87: Graduated Income Tax

context.text: Placed on the ballot by citizen initiative. The Blue Book lists 14 statewide measures on the November 3, 2026 ballot.

question.text: SHALL STATE TAXES BE INCREASED $2.7 BILLION ANNUALLY, IN ORDER TO INCREASE OR IMPROVE LEVELS OF PUBLIC SERVICES, INCLUDING K-12 PUBLIC SCHOOL EDUCATION, HEALTH CARE, AND EARLY CHILD CARE AND EDUCATION SERVICES, BY AN AMENDMENT TO THE COLORADO CONSTITUTION AND A CHANGE TO THE COLORADO REVISED STATUTES REPEALING EXISTING LAW AND CREATING NEW LAW TO REPLACE THE UNIFORM STATE INCOME TAX RATE WITH A GRADUATED INCOME TAX STRUCTURE, AND, IN CONNECTION THEREWITH, AMENDING THE TAXPAYER'S BILL OF RIGHTS TO ELIMINATE THE CONSTITUTIONAL REQUIREMENT FOR ALL TAXABLE NET INCOME TO BE TAXED AT ONE RATE WITH NO ADDED TAX ON INCOME; ESTABLISHING VARIOUS INCOME TAX RATES BASED ON THE AMOUNT OF TAXABLE INCOME EARNED BY INDIVIDUALS, ESTATES, TRUSTS, AND CORPORATIONS, WHILE MAINTAINING THE CURRENT 4.4% TAX ON INCOME FROM THE SALE OF A PRINCIPAL RESIDENCE, WHICH WILL RESULT IN THE ESTIMATED CHANGE IN INCOME TAXES OWED BY INDIVIDUALS AS IDENTIFIED IN THE FOLLOWING TABLE; AND AUTHORIZING THE STATE TO RETAIN AND SPEND ANY INCREASED REVENUE FROM THE NEW TAX STRUCTURE, AS A VOTER-APPROVED REVENUE CHANGE, TO SUPPLEMENT CURRENT LEVELS OF FUNDING FOR K-12 PUBLIC SCHOOL EDUCATION, HEALTH CARE, AND EARLY CHILD CARE AND EDUCATION PROGRAMS? (The ballot title is followed by a table of estimated changes in average income tax owed by income category, omitted here.)

summary.text: Replaces Colorado's flat 4.4 percent income tax with six graduated brackets starting in 2027: 3.7% on taxable income up to $25,000; 4.2% from $25,001 to $100,000; 4.4% from $100,001 to $500,000; 7.4% from $500,001 to $750,000; 7.9% from $750,001 to $1,000,000; and 8.4% above $1,000,000. Brackets are not adjusted for inflation. Additional revenue must go to K-12 education, health care, and early childhood care and education, supplementing rather than replacing current spending, and is exempt from the TABOR revenue limit. Per the Blue Book, taxpayers with Colorado taxable income below $510,834 would owe less (by up to $325) and those above would owe more. Fiscal impact: state revenue up an estimated $958.4 million in 2026-27 (half-year), $1.972 billion in 2027-28 and more later; the ballot title's maximum figure is $2.7 billion. The Blue Book notes that if Proposition 136 (4.4% rate cap) also passes, the outcome is unclear and would be resolved by the legislature or a court. Passes with a majority vote.

measure.yesMeans: Creates a graduated state income tax that increases revenue; uses the additional money for K-12 education, health care, and early childhood care and education; and exempts additional revenue collected from the state's constitutional revenue limit.
measure.noMeans: Keeps the current constitutional requirement for a flat state income tax rate.

argumentsFor.text: Blue Book argument for: "Amendment 87 cuts taxes for 97 percent of taxpayers, including most households and small businesses, while increasing taxes only for top earners who have the ability to pay."
Blue Book argument for: "The measure funds critical services at a time when additional funding is desperately needed."

argumentsAgainst.text: Blue Book argument against: "The measure is a multibillion-dollar tax increase, and hiking taxes on higher incomes will harm Colorado's economy."
Blue Book argument against: "The measure is an attack on the fair and predictable tax system that TABOR currently guarantees."

researchNotes: Source: the official 2026 Blue Book (Legislative Council Staff, nonpartisan), which gives the ballot title, the 'what your vote means' text, an analysis with arguments for and against, and the fiscal impact. Its 'for' and 'against' arguments are the staff's own summaries of the main arguments on each side, not statements from named campaigns; the booklet points to the Secretary of State's page for supporting and opposing organizations, which was not reviewed here. Ballotpedia is cited only for the certified-measure count. Ballotpedia notes a separate road-funding initiative was certified but withdrawn after its proponents reached an agreement with the state, so it is not on the ballot.
